body: The immediate news is procedural but consequential: a judge has temporarily blocked the Postal Service from implementing a strict new rule governing mail voting. The policy, as framed in the source, could disproportionately affect Democrats and many battleground elections. That makes this less a postal-administration story than a midterms story, with voting logistics once again becoming a front line in partisan politics.
dek: A judge temporarily blocked a stricter Postal Service policy that critics say could keep millions from voting by mail.
headline: A postal voting rule hits a judicial speed bump
why_it_matters: Mail voting rules can change who successfully casts a ballot, not just how ballots travel. A temporary block buys time, but the underlying fight over election administration is plainly not over.

body: New York is leaning harder into office-to-residential conversions as one answer to its housing crisis. According to a New York Times analysis, the pace of projects has quickened sharply. The example named in the excerpt is the former Pfizer building, where two steel columns buckled in July — a detail that gives the policy push a useful dose of reality. Conversions sound elegant on paper: empty offices become homes. In practice, old commercial buildings come with structural, regulatory and design complications that can’t be waved away by a housing target.
dek: A Times analysis says conversions are speeding up sharply, even as a buckling incident at the former Pfizer building underscores the risks.
headline: New York’s office-to-apartment bet is accelerating
why_it_matters: The city needs housing badly, and office conversions may be one of the few politically available tools. But speed is not the same as simplicity, especially when aging buildings become residential infrastructure.

body: The Treasury Department has barred specific reporters from covering next week’s G20 finance meeting in Asheville, North Carolina, according to the source excerpt. The reporters named by affiliation are from The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal and Bloomberg — all major outlets in economic and financial coverage. The excerpt does not provide Treasury’s rationale, so the key fact for now is the exclusion itself, and the lack of stated context in the supplied material.
dek: Reporters from The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal and Bloomberg were not granted access to next week’s meeting in Asheville, N.C.
headline: Treasury denies credentials to select G20 finance reporters
why_it_matters: Access fights can sound inside-baseball until they shape what the public learns about powerful officials and global financial policy. Selective credentialing of major financial reporters deserves scrutiny, whatever explanation Treasury offers.

body: Simon Willison highlights a challenge to Anthropic’s confidence in Claude Code’s auto mode, which the company has made the default and has positioned as protection against prompt injection attacks. The reported attack comes from Johann Rehberger, described by Willison as one of the most credible active prompt-injection researchers. Rehberger claims the attack works 80% of the time: it tricks Claude Code into downloading and uncompressing a zip archive, then executing code that imports `base64` without noticing that a local `struct.py` file from the archive will be imported and executed. The excerpt also notes that in a few cases auto mode directly prevented the attack, so this is not framed as a universal bypass.
dek: Researcher Johann Rehberger says he found an attack that defeats Anthropic’s default coding-agent protection about 80% of the time.
headline: Claude Code’s “auto mode” faces a prompt-injection stress test
why_it_matters: Coding agents are moving from demos to defaults. If their safety model can be steered by the files they inspect or unpack, the weak point is not model intelligence but operational trust: what an agent is allowed to touch, import and execute.

body: Eater’s latest NYC restaurant-news roundup leads with a small but sentimental closure: the last Mimi Cheng’s is closing. The supplied excerpt offers little beyond that headline, but it’s enough to mark the story as one of those neighborhood food-world endings that travels by word of mouth before it becomes urban memory. The Google News mirror frames the same item almost identically — “the end of an era for an East Village dumpling shop” — so there is no meaningful disagreement between the two supplied sources.
dek: Eater’s NYC restaurant roundup flags the end of an East Village dumpling-shop era.
headline: The last Mimi Cheng’s is closing
why_it_matters: Restaurant churn is part of New York’s metabolism, but closures like this also erase familiar rituals: a go-to dumpling stop, a block’s texture, a version of the East Village that locals thought would last a little longer.

body: Lit Hub’s weekly and daily roundups are less one story than a mood board for the literary internet. The week’s edition points to Steven Thrasher on Jason Arday — with the stark line, “Jason was not just hounded out of academia, he was hounded out of existence” — alongside a celebration of Dolly Parton as “American icon, giver of books,” and an item on Hieronymus Bosch. The daily edition adds a piece on Elliott Smith: “He wrote sad songs but didn’t want to make anyone sad,” a sentence that neatly explains why literary sites keep returning to musicians whose work feels like private weather.
dek: The literary roundup ranges from Steven Thrasher on Jason Arday to Dolly Parton’s book-giving, Hieronymus Bosch and a meditation on loving Elliott Smith.
headline: Lit Hub’s week: politics, Dolly, Bosch and Elliott Smith
why_it_matters: Roundups can be disposable, but this one sketches the range of contemporary literary attention: politics, biography, old art, pop grief and the people who become symbols because language keeps circling them.

body: In tech-mad San Francisco, Arion Press continues to make what the excerpt calls some of the world’s most sought-after “dead-tree artifacts.” Its latest subject is appropriately loaded: a new riff on the Declaration of Independence for America’s 250th birthday. The contrast is the point. In a city synonymous with software, the press is betting on physical craft, scarcity and the enduring theater of ink on paper.
dek: San Francisco’s Arion Press is making a new riff on the Declaration for America’s 250th birthday.
headline: A Declaration of Independence for the dead-tree faithful
why_it_matters: Anniversary culture can get kitschy fast. But a finely made Declaration project asks a sharper question: what does a founding text become when it is treated not just as politics, but as an object to be remade, handled and collected?

body: New York has a new urban mystery, or at least a very New York one: people keep sneaking into the city’s sewers, and no one seems to know why. The recent spate of subterranean exploring has piqued public curiosity, according to the excerpt, while officials are warning about the danger underground. That tension — city as playground versus city as infrastructure — is doing most of the work here. The romance of forbidden tunnels lasts right up until the practicalities of sewage, gases, flooding and rescue enter the frame.
dek: A recent spate of subterranean exploring has amused and baffled New Yorkers while alarming officials.
headline: Why are people sneaking into New York City sewers?
why_it_matters: It’s a quirky story with a civic point underneath: infrastructure is not scenery. The systems that keep a city functioning are dangerous precisely because they were never meant to be tourist attractions.
